title: Conformal Risk Control
research_question: Can conformal prediction be generalized from binary miscoverage control to finite-sample control of the expected value of arbitrary bounded monotone loss functions?
methodology: The authors formulate post-processing of a pretrained model as selecting a conservativeness parameter using calibration data and prove finite-sample expected-risk guarantees under exchangeability and monotonicity conditions. They derive extensions for distribution shift, quantile risk, multiple risks, adversarial risks, and U-statistic risks. The method is evaluated on four computer-vision and NLP tasks using 1,000 random data splits per task, with public datasets and released reproduction code.

key_findings.finding: For bounded losses that are non-increasing with a conservativeness parameter, the proposed calibration rule guarantees expected test loss at or below the user-specified risk level under the stated exchangeability assumptions.
The expected-risk guarantee generalizes ordinary conformal miscoverage control rather than merely reproducing prediction-set coverage.
Under additional i.i.d. continuity conditions, the method is shown to be tight up to an order-1/n term rather than becoming arbitrarily conservative.

Empirical experiments on segmentation, multilabel classification, hierarchical classification, and open-domain QA produced mean risks close to but below their specified targets across repeated random splits.
On Natural Questions, the F1-loss experiment with a target risk of 0.3 reported mean risk 0.2996 with standard deviation 0.0150 over 1,000 trials.
The framework can incorporate covariate shift through importance weighting and thereby extends weighted conformal prediction from miscoverage to general monotone risks.
Non-monotone losses cannot in general be passed directly to the basic conformal-risk rule, although the paper gives a monotone-envelope construction and an asymptotic alternative.

limitations: The primary finite-sample guarantee requires bounded losses and an appropriate monotonic relationship between the calibration parameter and loss.
The central guarantee is on expected risk rather than a per-instance, conditional, or high-probability guarantee over every calibration sample.
The main theorem relies on exchangeability; distribution-shift extensions require additional weighting information or assumptions.
Monotonizing a genuinely non-monotone loss can introduce conservativeness, while the alternative treatment is only asymptotically guaranteed and is most useful for near-monotone risks.
The authors leave more general unconditional control of some quantile-based risks, such as broader CVaR-type cases, unresolved.
The application studies demonstrate calibration behavior but do not establish that every operational loss relevant to deployment has the required mathematical structure.
raw_claims: Conformal risk control selects a model-output threshold using a calibration sample and a user-specified risk target.
The principal theorem controls the expected value of a bounded monotone loss on a new observation.
Ordinary conformal miscoverage is recovered as a special case of the framework.
The finite-sample correction approaches the requested risk level at order 1/n under additional regularity conditions.
The segmentation experiment used multiple open-source polyp-segmentation datasets and controlled false-negative rate.
The multilabel experiment used MS COCO and controlled false-negative rate.
The hierarchical ImageNet experiment controlled a graph-distance loss.
The Natural Questions experiment controlled a token-level F1-derived loss.
All four application examples were evaluated over 1,000 random splits.
A covariate-shift extension reweights calibration losses using the relationship between training and test distributions.
Direct application of the basic procedure to an arbitrary non-monotone loss does not provide the same guarantee.
The authors released code for reproducing the empirical examples.
